subject: english-language

moments.title: William Jones identifies Indo-European
moments.body: 2 February 1786: William Jones's address to the Asiatic Society. Sanskrit, Greek, Latin and other languages share a 'common source... no longer perhaps existing'. Comparative philology and the reconstruction of Proto-Indo-European begin.
moments.takeaway: Jones's insight launched modern historical linguistics. The Indo-European language family — covering most of Europe, Iran and northern India — has been one of the major intellectual reconstructions.

moments.title: Grimm's Law
moments.body: 1822: Grimm identifies the systematic sound change from Proto-Indo-European to Germanic languages. PIE *p > Germanic f (Latin pater, English father); PIE *t > Germanic θ (Latin tres, English three); PIE *k > Germanic h (Latin cor, English heart). Sound change is regular.
moments.takeaway: Grimm's Law was foundational. The Neogrammarian principle — sound change is exceptionless — has been refined but remains powerful.

moments.title: Causes of change
moments.body: Modern theories of language change include: internal (assimilation, simplification of unusual structures), external (contact, borrowing), social (covert prestige spreading non-standard forms), prestige imitation. Most changes have multiple causes.
moments.takeaway: Change is constant. English has been changing rapidly for 1,500 years and continues to do so.

now.title: Current change
now.body: Modern English changes observable in real time: 'literally' as intensifier (centuries old, currently expanding); 'like' as discourse marker (since 1980s); 'because + noun' ('because reasons'); 'they' as singular non-binary pronoun (rapidly accepted since 2010s).
now.open_questions: Are some changes irreversible? Most are. Some prescriptive rules hold off changes (split infinitives) for decades; eventually the standard usually catches up with general usage.

reflection: Language change is one of the most rigorously documented natural processes. The 200-year history of historical linguistics gives us tools to see English's continuing change as part of a long pattern — not decline, not chaos, but constant evolution.
